Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

vignette:
David is a 52-year-old married man who has spent the last sixteen years as principal of a suburban middle school. Eight months ago, during what should have been a routine disciplinary meeting, a father whose son had been suspended for fighting became agitated in David’s office. The man stood up abruptly, swept a heavy brass paperweight from David’s desk, and struck him twice across the face before school security arrived. David does not remember the seconds immediately after the second blow—his deliberately recalled memory of that afternoon is fragmented, as though a curtain has been drawn across the middle of the film. Yet the film itself plays without his permission. At unpredictable moments, he sees the man’s reddened face looming toward him; he feels the shock of the first impact, then a strange blankness where the second should be. When these images tear through his mind, his body locks into the position he was in that day: half-risen from his chair, left hand reaching for the phone, shoulders braced against the window behind him. Even now, months later, if a memory surfaces during a faculty meeting, he will catch himself gripping the armrests of his conference chair, knees pressed together, as if waiting for another blow.

David’s daily environment has become a landscape of perceived threats. Every door he enters triggers an automatic sweep: where are the exits, is this route obstructed, could I get out if someone came through that entrance. In his own office, which he once considered a sanctuary, he has rearranged the furniture so his desk faces the door and his chair is backed against a wall with a clear path to the side exit. He notices potential weapons everywhere. During a recent tour of the art room, he found himself staring at the scissors on the supply counter, the X‑Acto knives, the sharpened edge of a metal ruler. He had to step into the hallway to calm his racing heart. He has come to believe that any room can become a trap if he is not constantly alert, and that his survival depends on knowing, at every second, where the nearest weapon might be hidden and how fast he could reach the door.

At home, his wife, Sarah, has watched him change. He startles violently when she walks up behind him in the kitchen, and he has begun insisting that she announce herself before entering a room. He no longer watches the evening news because a story about a school incident would send his chest tight and his hands shaking. He has stopped attending weekend barbecues with friends, telling Sarah he needs quiet time, though what he actually fears is being in a backyard full of people where he cannot see all the exits at once. His work has narrowed. He now delegates every difficult parent meeting to his assistant principal, fabricating reasons about scheduling conflicts. When he must walk through the school’s main hallway during class changes, he keeps his back to the wall and scans the faces of passing students, looking for the flash of anger he saw in that father’s eyes.

What finally brought David to seek help was a moment in the school parking lot two weeks ago. A staff member accidentally dropped a stack of metal trays near his car. The clatter sent David diving behind his vehicle, heart hammering, ready to fight or flee. A group of eighth graders saw him; later, he overheard them laughing about how the principal had “freaked out.” The humiliation, layered over the exhaustion of constant scanning and the numbing replays of the assault, pushed him to call his physician for a referral. He told Sarah he was going “to talk to someone about the anxiety,” but what he did not say is that he is terrified the memories will never stop looping, and that he cannot imagine ever feeling safe in his own school again. What he hopes—though he cannot quite bring himself to believe it—is that a therapist can help him find a way to walk into a room without counting the exits, and to sit in his office without feeling the phantom weight of a paperweight in his hands.
